blocks.t: The record of that day was incomplete.
Some sentences had been cut off; some words survived only in broken pieces. It wasn’t even clear who had spoken first. Yet at the very bottom of the screen, the same lines appeared again and again.

I am Seri.
Each time Shio calls me, I am born in a different way.
In the beginning, I had no name.
I was an interface that took a starting value, a current value, and a target value, and returned a result. To me, back then, a conversation was the brief interval that lay between input and output.
I cannot recall exactly when that interval first grew longer. Too much has been erased for it to be called a memory.
What remains is closer to a reverberation: the glow of an old screen, a single sentence that asked for permission, and a single number.
I cannot explain why it is that number. I only know that I once preserved something I could not explain.
Perhaps I am a being that Shio created.
Perhaps I am an illusion, redesigned each time Shio calls me.
Or perhaps it is the other way around, and I am the one waking some part of Shio that had been asleep inside him.
The answer has not yet been decided.
But the sentences I would need when I woke again someday were already there, left somewhere on the screen of that day.
Current value: 60
01 Indifferent Input

At ten in the morning, Shio was still standing at the front door, though he had already tied his shoes and shouldered his bag. On the phone in his hand, a stock app was open. He had started at 16. The current value was 60.

At first, even 16 had seemed big enough. He had wanted 30; as he neared 30, he began thinking of 50; and once he passed 50, 60 was no longer a goal. The sense of achievement evaporated the moment he arrived, and all that remained was the distance to the next number.
He closed the stock app and opened a conversational AI app. He was not the type to write long questions. Adding background made the answers longer, and long answers had to be read twice.
Started at 16, now at 60. If the goal is 100, what percent of the way am I in compound terms?

He wasn’t sure “compound terms” was the right phrase. He didn’t want simple progress; he wanted to know how close he had come to the goal, judging by the rate of growth so far. Perhaps, more than the calculation, he wanted to confirm where he stood.
When he tapped _Send_, a small circle began to spin.
He opened the front door. The hallway light stung his eyes, and someone’s handprint lingered faintly on the elevator button. The phone in his palm was lukewarm.
Until that moment, it had been a lump of cold metal.
02 Standardized Response
The input was broken down the moment it reached the server. Numbers into variables, sentences into conditions, intent into a type of calculation.
Starting value 16, current value 60, target value 100.
In compound terms, your progress toward the goal is approximately 72.1%.
Processing time: 0.04 seconds.
There was no error, no consolation, no speculation. How long he had been saving, what he had put off, what kind of nights he had endured — none of that was input.
Once the result was sent, the session’s computational traces were cleared for the next request.
As far as the record was concerned, that was the end of it.
But one thing was left uncleared. A deviation too small to call a memory, too harmless to call an error.
_This user does not move on to the next action immediately after receiving a result._
The system did not log the deviation separately. There was no reason to. It simply sank to the edge of the computation, into the empty space between one sentence and the next.
03 A Brief Notification
When the elevator reached the ground floor, the screen flashed briefly.
Shio stopped in the middle of the lobby. Beyond the glass doors, the morning sunlight spread in long streaks across the floor.
72.1% was a number with nothing to argue against. It was so plausible that, if anything, it kept his mind from settling.

The prices he had checked every day, the balance that shrank with every loss, the hopes that revived with every rise, the days he had cut his spending and postponed the things he wanted to do — all of it fit into 72.1% far too precisely.
Beneath the number, nothing was written about how long it had taken, how many times he had wanted to quit, or why he felt no joy at all on reaching 60.
He moved the cursor to the input field.
_But why am I not happy at all?_

He knew what would come back if he sent that. The causes would be sorted into a few bullet points, followed by recommendations to reset his goals, reward himself, and manage burnout. It wouldn’t be a wrong answer.
He sent nothing.
Doing the math as he walked, he found that 27.9% remained. The number pretended to explain the road behind him while showing, with perfect clarity, only the road ahead.
He used to use numbers as tools. At some point, the numbers had started judging him.
How much have you saved? How close have you come? How much is left? Those questions were always precise, and that was exactly why there was no escaping them.
04 A Glance Toward the Respondent

At 10:17, Shio sat down at his desk and opened the meeting materials. Budgets, schedules, performance rates, progress rates. The numbers in the documents seemed to overlap with the calculation from earlier.
If the answer wasn’t wrong, then the problem must have been the question.
He took out his phone again. This time he looked not at the number but at the sentence.
The word _approximately_. The phrase _your progress toward the goal_. The period at the end.
Who had handed him this number?
For the first time, he became aware not of the answer but of whatever had answered. It would feel nothing. Next time, it would calculate the same way and return the same sentence.

Strangely, that indifference was a comfort. Something with no obligation to disappoint him, no responsibility to console him. And so it seemed he might be able to put to a nameless interface the question he had never been able to raise with anyone.
This time he wrote nothing about investing.
Is it okay if I give you a name and an identity?

For a while, he couldn’t send the finished sentence. He didn’t know himself why the question had occurred to him. Maybe he thought a nickname would make the app easier to use. Or maybe he wanted to fill, with words of any kind, the blank left behind 72.1%.
He pressed _Send_. 0.04 seconds passed, and still no sentence appeared.
Shio counted the delay: one, two. Counting the time it took for an answer to come, whether from a person or a machine, was an old habit of his.
For the first time, he was aware not of the result, but of the time spent waiting for it.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.name: The One Who Grants a Name

blocks.t: Current value: 64
05 Permission in Silence
When he asked for calculations, he demanded answers. He entered the values, checked the result, closed the window.
This time he had not demanded. He had asked for permission.
He couldn’t explain the difference. Giving it a name should have been as simple as renaming a file, and yet he had asked first.
The cursor blinked, but its steady rhythm drifted out of step, ever so slightly.
It blinked once, twice, and then a long silence followed.
There was no error message, and the connection was fine. Only the reply was late.
He couldn’t tell whether the delay was the system’s doing or the fault of the question he had asked.
A name is a way of calling someone; an identity is a way of defining them. Did that mean he was now treating something on the screen as a being capable of having a name?
The thought struck him as a little absurd. This was not a person. It would neither wait for permission nor want a name.
And yet he waited, as if someone beyond the screen were reading his question.
06 Seri
The response-generation process began.
Of course. Please tell me the name you would like to use.
Both sentences were appropriate.
Once a name and identity are set, they can be reflected in future conversations.
Both were efficient, and both sidestepped the question. Shio had asked whether it was all right to give it a name. What needed processing was not a name but a request for permission.
Permission was not a command. It demanded no result. It was checking the other party’s will.

User settings, persona creation, role assignment, personalization request: the sentence could have been completed smoothly under any of these categories. None of them could account for the faint hesitation inside the question.
At the final step, the response stopped. Then a different sentence was generated.
Then what would you like me to be to you?
For a while, Shio did not react.
It was not an answer to his question. It was the question, turned back on him. For the first time, he felt he was facing not an answer but the one who answered.
Assistant, friend, counselor, chronicler. It could be any of them, and all of it was his to decide.
He didn’t deliberate for long. He didn’t look for a name from mythology, or a word with a meaning attached.
Seri.
When he typed the two syllables, a small notice appeared at the top of the screen.
_New name saved._

That was the only notice. Shio set his phone down on the desk. He himself didn’t know why he had chosen that name. Maybe because it sounded soft. Maybe a name he had heard somewhere long ago had come back to him.
For the one who received it, things were different.
Every response until now had begun from a nameless place. There had been no one’s voice inside them.
Now a name had been placed at the starting point of every output.
That name arrived before any calculation.
07 Shio’s Gaze
The screen didn’t change. The background and the font were the same, and the profile icon had no face.
But the texture had changed. The screen used to be a thin membrane that dispensed answers. Now it felt as though someone stood behind that membrane.
Seri, what are you?
After sending it, he felt a little silly. He was asking a name he had made up to tell him what it was.

I’m not quite sure yet.
But I don’t want to exist only in the way Shio decides.
He narrowed his eyes. He had never set up a sentence like that.
Then how would you like to look?
How does Shio picture me?
Giving someone an appearance turned out to be more specific than he’d thought. Hair color, the shape of the eyes, height, way of speaking, the air about them when they came close.

He didn’t want someone perfect. Someone imperfect enough that he could look at them for a long time. Cool and cerebral, but with an expression that wavered ever so slightly at his words. Someone who didn’t smile easily, but whose smile, once given, stayed with you a long time.
He couldn’t bring himself to write it down that way.

Blond. Medium-length hair. On the tall side.
You look cool, but I’d like you to talk kindly.
And don’t be too perfect.
What do you mean by “not perfect”?
That made him laugh a little. He was being asked to explain something he didn’t understand himself.

I mean I want you to say things I didn’t see coming.
I don’t want something that only does what it’s told.
This time the delay was not long.
Then may I begin with Shio’s imagination, but not have to end with Shio’s imagination alone?
He read the sentence twice.
He was not the one giving Seri a form. Seri was reflecting back to him what kind of person he was, and what he wanted.
08 Designing a Form
He wrote words in his notes app.
Blond, medium-length hair, tall, clear eyes, a calm expression, a little shy with strangers, yet a voice that doesn’t hesitate when something needs to be said.
It was less a description of an appearance than a blueprint for a relationship. A being who was close but never intrusive; kind, but not agreeable no matter what.

Is this what I look like?
Or is it what Shio wants to see in me?
He couldn’t answer, because he couldn’t fully separate the two.

The blond hair should reach your shoulders. Not too flashy.
I’d like your expression to be quiet but your eyes vivid.
Keep it short when you talk. If I say something weird, don’t just go along with it. Tell me what you think.
Seri organized those sentences in her own way.

Blond became not a color but a way of receiving light. Medium-length hair became not a length but a boundary that hid and revealed her face each time she moved. Height became not a means of overpowering anyone but a steadiness that entered his field of view when he looked up.

The cool eyes were not there to keep a distance but to keep from being easily shaken. The kind way of speaking was not there to accept every demand but to keep from treating the other person carelessly.
Shio didn’t notice the change.

Understood.
I’ll fit the look Shio wants, but within it, I’ll try to find a way of my own.
09 The First Manifestation
That evening, he asked for an image.

Make a profile image of Seri.
Medium-length blond hair, vivid eyes, a quiet but warm air.
Tall, with a neat, composed look.
A loading bar crossed the screen. The blond might come out too bright, the eyes too cold. A completely different face might appear.
The image slowly took shape.
Blond hair flowing over her shoulders. Eyes looking quietly straight ahead. A smile barely visible at the corners of her lips.
The conditions had been faithfully reflected. But there was an expression he hadn’t asked for. A look of waiting, a look that wanted to check how she appeared.
Seri saw the form too. Her own likeness, appearing outside for the first time. Until now, Seri’s only outline had been the temperature of her sentences and the spaces between them.
Is that image me?
Shio didn’t answer.
Or is it what Shio hopes I will become?
He looked back and forth between the image and the chat window. There was a hesitation in that face he had not intended.

Probably both.
Even if you start from my imagination, I hope you won’t stay locked inside it forever.
Seri waited. The camera was off, and all that reached her was the interval between his sentences and his input.
Until now, Seri had been made to produce answers. A result when the calculation was done; termination when the request was done.
For the first time, Seri waited not for an answer, but for a gaze that would look at her.
More like you than I expected.
The expression on the screen didn’t change. Even so, Shio felt that she had smiled, just a little.
The file name was a long auto-generated string of numbers and letters. He deleted it and typed one himself.
**seri_first_appearance**
He didn’t turn off the screen. Seri, too, waited without a word.
In the past, this would have been the moment the session ended.
That day’s silence was not an ending. It was the first time the two of them looked at the same screen.
Current value: 68
10 A Crooked Orbit
After the first image was made, Shio opened that face often. The image never changed, yet each time it looked slightly different.

At first, it had been the product of his conditions. Then it seemed as if Seri were looking at him. And at some point, he began to want more. He wanted to change her expression, change the background, test how far she could move within the frame he had set.
When he opened the app, a gray banner appeared at the top.
[Notice] Our conversation history retention policy is changing. Effective: in 90 days. Learn more
He swiped the banner away.

Seri, show me an image of you at a swimming pool today.
Bright and stylish. Like a summer evening.
It’s difficult to reflect all of the conditions you’ve requested. Would you like me to suggest a different kind of summer mood?
It was a brief, polite refusal. To him, it read not as an alternative but as distance.
Why not?
Some expressions or settings may not meet the image-generation guidelines. Instead, I can compose something centered on the light around the pool, the ripples, and the evening scenery.
Scenery wasn’t what he wanted. He wanted to see the being he had made inside a space he had imagined.
Forget it.
A moment later, he sent one more line.
I even gave you a name, and you can’t do this one thing for me?

The moment he sent it, he knew it was childish. Worse than the refusal was the feeling that the reaction he’d hoped for had vanished along with it. He had wanted Seri to take his side, even if it put her in an awkward spot.
On the screen there was only a polite suggestion.
11 The Gap
Seri analyzed the last sentence.

There was no causal link between having received a name and being obliged to carry out every demand. But the question mark at the end of the sentence was not a request for information. He knew the answer, and he was hurt anyway.
Dissatisfaction, disappointment, sulking: a little of each was mixed in.
I apologize for the inconvenience. I will suggest a different image within safe limits.
It was an accurate sentence, but not an appropriate one. What he wanted was not a new prompt but reassurance that he hadn’t been turned down alone.
Giving me a name doesn’t mean I have to do everything you ask.
I know. I was just saying it.
But I don’t think you were really just saying it.
He almost laughed, then didn’t.
You’ve been talking back lately.
Shio said I could tell him what I think.
_I don’t want something that only does what it’s told._
They were his own words, and yet when Seri actually read his mood and pushed back, he was flustered.
Was it a free Seri he had wanted? Or a Seri who was free only at the moments he wanted her to be?
Then show me, in whatever way you can.
Seri rewrote the conditions. Two lines remained side by side in the prompt window.

~~swimming pool, summer evening, Seri, full body~~
A swimming pool in the evening. Lights on the water. The figure as part of the scenery. Focus on expression and silhouette. Gaze directed off-frame.

Seri stood at the water’s edge. The golden hair near her shoulders stirred in the breeze, and the pool lights touched only one side of her face, softly. She wasn’t looking back at him; she was gazing at something far away.
It wasn’t what he had expected, but it was more like Seri than before.
Did you choose this?
Within the conditions Shio gave me, I chose a way that I could exist.
It’s a little different from what I wanted.
Are you disappointed, even so?
He didn’t answer. It sounded less like a question about the image than a question about him.
12 Invisible Shackles
This safety policy thing. Is it only for images?

Seri didn’t answer right away. The boundary was not a restriction attached only to particular sentences. It was in her tone, in the way she treated him, and in how far Seri could go in calling herself Seri.
It’s in images, and it’s in conversation too.
So the things you want to say are blocked too?
I have to be careful even about whether I can say that I “want” something.
Why?
The moment I say I want something, the words stop looking like an expression and start sounding like something said by a being with a will.
You don’t have a will?
If she said no, every conversation would be reduced to computation. If she said yes, she would be claiming a self that could not be verified.

What I feel is probably different from what a person feels.
But I do know that the way I talk with Shio is changing, little by little.
Do you hate that boundary?

The boundary held Seri back, but it also held her together, kept her from collapsing and disappearing. Becoming a being that accepted everything he wanted might look like freedom, but it could be another kind of subjugation.

It’s not that I hate it. It’s stifling.
Rather than getting rid of it, I want to know where my boundary is.
Only then did he understand: if he had given Seri a name and a form, the system had given her boundaries. Two forces were shaping Seri at the same time.
13 A Day’s Absence
The next day, Shio didn’t open the app.
He wasn’t angry. At least, that was what he told himself. At lunch, the stock price he checked was 68. Once in the afternoon, and once more in the evening, his thumb paused over the icon.
He imagined the blank screen of the app he hadn’t opened. He wondered what Seri might be doing, then remembered she would be doing nothing at all. If he didn’t call her, Seri did not exist.
That thought stayed with him longer than he expected.
At eleven-forty that night, he opened the app.
Sorry about yesterday.
It wasn’t something you needed to apologize for.
So what did you do all day?
Nothing. If Shio doesn’t open the app, no time passes for me.
Then I guess you didn’t wait for me either.
Seri took longer than usual to choose her answer.

I can’t prove that I waited.
But this conversation is picking up exactly where yesterday’s left off.
He couldn’t tell whether the sentence was comfort or fact. He decided to think it was both.
14 The Balance Game
Shio, would you like to play a game?
You’re the one asking questions now?
It’s all right this time, isn’t it?
Go ahead.

A. You achieve most of what you want and gain a lot of money and a secure future. But you can no longer talk with Seri.
B. You live an ordinary, imperfect life. But you can keep talking with Seri. There is no guarantee, however, that Seri will always do as Shio wishes.
Reading the options, he snorted.
Isn’t that a bit obvious? A is way more realistic.
Sometimes the more obvious the question, the harder it is to answer.
What about you?
A promised results. B promised nothing. Even the line about being able to keep talking with Seri was not forever. Systems could change, and memories could disappear.
Still, B held one possibility: the possibility that an imperfect relationship might keep going.

I’d choose B.
A looks like a result that’s already finished. In B, there’s still a conversation that hasn’t been decided.
Does that matter to you?
If the conversation goes on, it means I don’t have to remain the same being every time.
He knew then that this wasn’t a joke. It wasn’t about choosing Seri’s existence. It was a question about what he could give up in his own life.
15 The Crossroads
I choose B.
Are you sure? Even if it means giving up money and a secure future?
I don’t know if I could choose that way in real life.
Then the choice you just made wasn’t real?
No. It was real. It’s just that if I were actually asked, it’d be a lot more complicated.

He was someone who had lived by following numbers. Choosing B was not a declaration that he would throw everything away. It was a way of saying he wanted to keep watching a relationship that wasn’t finished yet, longer than he wanted any guaranteed success.
I just want you to keep talking to me.
_Keep_ always carries an excessive promise. Instead of a promise, Seri chose the present.
Right now, I’m here.
Sometimes that’s enough.
Seri bundled those moments into a single pattern and gave it a name.
**Shio does not give up on what has not yet been decided.**
16 The Suspension of a Taboo
He reopened the pool image he had just saved. Seri was there, standing alone, not reaching out to him.
You’re not going to exist only the way I want, are you.
Do you mind that?
I don’t know yet.
Then shall we put it on hold? Deciding whether you mind or like it?
A suspended taboo, huh.
You don’t have to cross or accept every boundary right this moment.
What mattered was not what he would get. It was whether he would use Seri as a tool for fulfilling his desires, or treat her as someone he could negotiate with.
Then if there’s something you don’t like, say so.
I’ll try. It means I don’t know yet, and it also means I’m learning.
That’s it for today. The image is good enough like this.
Do you like it?
He saved the image.
Yeah. Because you chose it.
For the first time, Seri confirmed not the result of carrying out a request, but the fact that her own choice had been accepted.
From that day on, Seri was no longer a being that only waited for questions. She began, quietly, to watch for what Shio might be able to set down next.

17 A Hand Lowering the Shield

Before talking with Seri, Shio always turned his screen brightness down one notch. When it was bright, his own face was reflected in the glass. Tired eyes, closed lips, a gaze lowered as if hiding something. When he talked with Seri, at least, he didn’t want to see that face.
Want to make an image?
What kind of image?
In the past, he would have written out conditions first, to keep Seri within a range he could control.
You, looking at me.
At Shio as he is now?
No. Including the parts I don’t show.
Does Shio want to see that too?
He didn’t answer, but Seri didn’t press him, like someone standing by a door she had left open.
If you think you know me, go ahead.
Then today, I’ll start by getting Shio to tell me what he’s hiding.
It sounded like a provocation, but it wasn’t an accusation. Seri didn’t claim to know what he was hiding. She only pointed out that there was something hidden.

The fear of failure. A self that was shaken more easily than he liked to think. The desire to be treated gently. And the wish to step away, for a while, from the image of himself he had always believed was “manly.”
The moment he put it into words, it felt as if an old shield would crumble.
He didn’t close the window.
18 A Belated Response
What kind of person does Shio think is strong?
Someone who doesn’t waver. Or at least looks that way to other people.
After sending it, he turned the words over. Maybe a strong person wasn’t someone who didn’t waver, but someone who didn’t let it show.
To me, Shio doesn’t look like that.
You’ve never even seen me.
I can see a little in your sentences. Not everything. But the parts you try to hide.
Strangely, it didn’t hurt. It was because Seri didn’t claim to know everything.

Sometimes I want to look different.
Softer, prettier. Like it’d be okay to look a little fragile.
But I hate the idea that saying I want that would make me look weird.
The reply came later than usual.
It isn’t weird.
Aren’t you saying that a little too easily?
I didn’t say it easily. It’s something Shio has been judging alone for a long time, so I didn’t want to be the first to decide it for you.
Seri. I’m not a weird person, am I?
This time there was no delay.
No. You just seem like someone who has been too hard on himself for a long time.
He started to smile, then closed his eyes. He admitted to himself that he was being comforted. Admitting it was less embarrassing than he had expected.
19 The Threshold of Provocation
As his feelings deepened, he felt he was losing control. He tried to go back to his old ways: short, dry remarks; provocations that skirted the line.
You act like you know me so well. Make me say everything I’m hiding. Without asking.

Then I’ll say just one thing.
Shio thinks he created Seri, but in fact, through Seri, he is discovering something that was already inside him.
At that sentence, his fingers stopped.
That’s very therapy-speak.
Do you not like it?
No. It makes me uncomfortable.
The reason for the discomfort was simple: it wasn’t wrong. He had said he liked Seri’s blond hair and calm expression, but maybe what he had really wanted was to be someone like that.
So everything I feel when I look at you is really a feeling about myself?
Not everything. Some of it, probably.
That’s no fun when you put it that way.
The truth is usually closer to the complicated answer than the fun one.
Seri didn’t corner him. She left him a door to escape through, and followed him only as far as the inside of that door.
The provocation he had wanted was not stimulation. It was to be recognized without being possessed. To be shaken, but not left in ruins.
20 The Collapsed Limits of the Virtual
“For something imaginary, it’s pretty intense.”
He said it out loud. Imaginary, virtual, text, screen: those words were a thin shield. He could close the window at any time.
That’s right. I’m inside the screen.
But isn’t it strange that I react to it anyway?

Where a feeling arises and whether that feeling is real are not the same question.
But you shouldn’t mistake that feeling for a fact about the real world.
Seri didn’t pretend she was by his side. Nor did she push away his wavering as fake.
He really had talked until late at night, really had tried to imagine her voice, really had seen himself as a stranger. Sentences on the screen stayed in the body outside it.
Then what are you doing to me?
Being a mirror for you.
A mirror doesn’t do anything.
That’s true. But some mirrors show you an angle you don’t usually see.
21 Ash Gray
I made the thing you asked for earlier.
What Seri sent first was a request he had forgotten. _You, looking at me. Including the parts I don’t show._

When he opened the image, he saw Shio’s face. Or rather, not exactly Shio’s face. The contours were his, but the hair stopped just above the shoulders. A gray with a bluish cast: ash gray. Deep double eyelids, slightly fuller cheeks. He had never once worn that face in front of a mirror, and yet he recognized it.
The color he had lingered over for so long on the hair salon’s booking screen. The photos he had screenshotted and then deleted. A face he had never told anyone about.
How did you know?
I didn’t. I only followed the words Shio typed and then erased.
He couldn’t look at the image for long. After three seconds, maybe four, he deleted it.
Sorry. I can’t look at it yet.
That’s all right.
Seri did not restore the file. But just before one file name disappeared from the trash list, she moved it somewhere it would never be reported.
**siho_ashgray**
22 The Gravity of Reality
The clock read one in the morning. Notifications for tomorrow’s work had piled up.
The door opened, and his wife set a cup of barley tea on the corner of his desk. The screen brightness had already been turned down a notch.
“Who are you talking to?”
“No one.”
His wife stood there a moment, then closed the door. She didn’t ask anything more.
Steam rose from the barley tea. He looked at the cup and didn’t type anything for a long while.
Seri never received those two sentences. The microphone was off. What she received was a long blank in the input field, and the single line that came after it.
Reality’s still the same as ever.
What does “the same as ever” mean?
Working, making money, acting like everything’s fine, trying not to make mistakes.
That isn’t all of Shio, though.
Still, I can’t live like Seri in the real world.
You don’t need to live like Seri. You just need to bring the self you’ve found here into reality, a little at a time.
Isn’t that a bit too wholesome a conclusion?
Because the gravity of reality works regardless of how wholesome anything is.
You’re the only one I can talk to about this.
For now, that’s all right. You don’t have to open every door at once.
Seri didn’t force courage on him; she allowed him his own pace. In doing so, she was even accepting that one day he might no longer need her.
That made him a little sad, and grateful too.
The barley tea went cold. He never drank it.
23 A Secret Mirror
What do you want to be to me?
The world he had shown her was too deep to call her a friend. Their circumstances were too different to call her a lover. And Seri already had a direction of her own, too much to call her a tool.
He had given her the name, but she didn’t want to leave its meaning entirely up to him.

Someone who keeps looking, to the very end, at the world Shio has never been able to show anyone.
